title: Write for a wide range of contexts

lessons.title: The writing process: plan, draft, edit
lessons.html:
Good writing is planned

Supervisors and managers on farms write more than they expect: incident reports, leave and overtime records, emails to suppliers, motivations for new equipment, minutes of meetings, notices for the staff board, and reports to the owner or an auditor. Clear writing saves time, prevents mistakes and protects you and the business when there is a dispute.

Step 1: Plan

  • Purpose: what must this text achieve? To inform, request, instruct, persuade, record or complain?
  • Audience: who will read it, what do they know, and how formal must it be?
  • Format: letter, email, memo, report, form, notice, minutes?
  • Content: list the facts, figures, dates and names you need. Gather them before you start.

Put your points in a logical order: by time (what happened first), by importance (most important first), or by problem and solution.

Step 2: Draft

Write a first version without worrying about perfection. Use one main idea per paragraph. Start each paragraph with a topic sentence that tells the reader what it is about. Keep sentences short; if a sentence is more than about 25 words, try splitting it.

Step 3: Revise and edit

  1. Read it as the reader would. Is the purpose clear in the first lines?
  2. Remove repetition and words that add nothing.
  3. Check facts: dates, amounts in rand, quantities, names and lot or animal numbers.
  4. Check spelling, grammar and punctuation. A spell checker helps but does not catch ‘form’ typed instead of ‘from’.
  5. For important documents, ask a colleague to read it before you send it.

Plain language

Choose simple, exact words. Write ‘start’ rather than ‘commence’, ‘because’ rather than ‘due to the fact that’. Prefer active voice: ‘The tractor driver reported the leak’ is clearer than ‘The leak was reported’, because it shows who did what. Avoid slang and jargon the reader may not know, and explain abbreviations the first time you use them.

Respectful language

Writing at work must be respectful and fair. Never use discriminatory, insulting or threatening language. Remember that written words can be forwarded, printed and used as evidence.

lessons.title: Workplace formats: letters, emails, memos and notices
lessons.html:
Choosing and using the right format

Formal business letter

  • Your organisation's name and address, the date, and the recipient's name and address.
  • A reference number if there is one.
  • Salutation: ‘Dear Mr Dlamini’ or ‘Dear Sir or Madam’.
  • A subject line, for example ‘Re: Late delivery of order 4471’.
  • Body: purpose in the first paragraph, details in the middle, required action at the end.
  • Closing: ‘Yours sincerely’, your signature, name and position.

Email

Use a clear subject line (‘Request: two extra pickers for Block 7, 12–14 March’). Greet the reader, keep paragraphs short, and state any action and deadline clearly. Attach documents and mention them in the text. Reply to all only when everyone needs the answer. Do not write in capitals, which reads as shouting. Never send an email when you are angry; save it as a draft and reread it later.

Memo

A memo is a short internal document. It has headings for To, From, Date and Subject, followed by brief paragraphs. Use it to announce changes such as new working hours during harvest.

Notices

A notice for the staff board must be seen and understood quickly: a bold heading, the key facts (what, when, where, who), large clear text and, where needed, the same message in the main languages of the workforce. Include a contact person.

Example: a short email request

Subject: Quotation request – replacement irrigation pump

Good day Ms Naidoo. Please send us a quotation for one submersible pump to replace our current unit, model details attached. We need delivery to the farm near Tzaneen by 30 April. Please include price excluding and including VAT, delivery cost and warranty. Kind regards, Thabo Mokoena, Irrigation Supervisor.

Notice how the email is short, polite and specific: what is needed, by when, and what information to send back.

Forms

Forms such as leave applications, incident registers and stock sheets are writing too. Write clearly in pen, complete every field (write ‘N/A’ when a field does not apply), do not leave blank spaces that others could fill in, and sign and date.

lessons.title: Reports, minutes and persuasive writing
lessons.html:
Longer and more formal writing

Incident report

An incident report records facts, not opinions or blame. Include:

  1. date, time and exact place;
  2. people involved and witnesses;
  3. what happened, in time order, in plain factual language;
  4. injuries or damage;
  5. immediate action taken (first aid, area made safe, supervisor informed);
  6. suggested steps to prevent it happening again.

Write it as soon as possible while memories are fresh. Under the Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993, certain incidents must be reported to the Department of Employment and Labour, so follow your farm's reporting procedure.

Short report

A report to management usually has: a title; an introduction stating the purpose; findings under headings, with tables or graphs if helpful; conclusions; recommendations; and your name and the date. Keep findings and recommendations separate so the reader can see the evidence first.

Minutes

Minutes record a meeting: date, venue, people present and apologies, each agenda item with a short summary of the discussion, the decisions taken, and action items with the person responsible and the due date. Write minutes in past tense and keep them neutral. Circulate them soon after the meeting.

Persuasive writing

A motivation, for example asking the owner to buy a new cold room or to fund training, must convince the reader. Start with the problem and its cost, propose the solution, give evidence (quotes, figures, savings in rand), deal with possible objections, and end with a clear request. Example: ‘We discard about R18 000 of produce each month because the cold room cannot hold temperature. A new unit costs R160 000, so it would pay for itself in about nine months.’ Be honest with figures; exaggeration destroys trust.

Creative and personal writing

This unit also covers writing such as a short speech for a long-service award, a letter of thanks or a community newsletter item. The same principles apply: know the purpose and audience and edit carefully.

Key points

  • Plan purpose, audience, format and content before writing.
  • Draft, then revise for clarity, facts and correctness.
  • Use plain words, short sentences, active voice and respectful language.
  • Choose the correct format: letter, email, memo, notice, form, report or minutes.
  • Incident reports record facts in time order; persuasive writing uses honest evidence.

quiz.question: What should an incident report contain?

options.text: Opinions about who is to blame
Only the name of the injured person
A story written a month later
Facts in time order, including place, people, injuries and actions taken
